title: Sliding Window
tagline: Turn O(n²) brute-force scans of contiguous subarrays into O(n) with a moving left/right pointer.
intro:
The sliding window pattern maintains a **contiguous range** `[left, right]` over an array or string and slides it forward, updating an aggregate (sum, count, frequency map) incrementally instead of recomputing from scratch. That incremental update is the magic: every element enters the window once and leaves once, so the whole scan is O(n) even though it conceptually examines many subarrays.

Use it whenever a problem says **"contiguous subarray" or "substring"** plus a condition — longest, shortest, or a fixed size. The brute force enumerates all O(n²) windows; the sliding window reuses work between adjacent windows to get O(n).

This module gives you the three concrete templates — fixed-size, longest-variable, and shortest-variable — and the decision rule that tells you which one a prompt wants.
objectives: Spot the 'contiguous subarray/substring + condition' signal that means sliding window
Apply the fixed-size window template for 'window of size k' problems
Apply the grow/shrink template for longest-valid-window problems
Apply the shrink-to-minimum template for shortest-valid-window problems
Maintain a window frequency map for substring/anagram problems
Explain why each element is added and removed at most once → O(n)

signals: "Longest / shortest / maximum / minimum" window meeting a condition
"At most k distinct", "no repeating characters" → variable window with a counter
antiSignals: Subsequence (not contiguous) → usually DP, not a window
Need a pair from a sorted array → two pointers from both ends
Order doesn't matter / set membership → hashing

sections.heading: The big idea in plain words
sections.body:
Imagine watching a street through a bus window. As the bus rolls forward, one new shop slides into view and one old shop slides out - you never re-scan the whole street each second, you just account for the one that entered and the one that left. A sliding window keeps a running total the same lazy way.

Example: the sum of every 3 numbers in a row in `[2, 1, 5, 1, 3]`. Start with 2 + 1 + 5 = 8. To slide one step right, subtract the 2 that left and add the 1 that entered, giving 7. Slide again: subtract 1, add 3, giving 9. Each move is a single add and a single subtract instead of re-adding three numbers from scratch.

sections.heading: What a window is
sections.body:
A window is the range `[left, right]` (inclusive) currently under consideration, plus a running summary of what's inside it.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **right** | Expands the window by including a new element each iteration |
| **left** | Contracts the window when the condition is violated |
| **window state** | The aggregate kept in sync: sum, count, or a frequency map |
| **valid window** | One that satisfies the problem's condition |

The invariant you maintain: *after processing each `right`, the window state exactly reflects the elements in `[left, right]`.* Keep that true and the logic stays simple.

sections.heading: Which template? (decision flow)
sections.body:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A["Contiguous range + condition"] --> B{"Fixed size k given?"}
  B -- Yes --> C["Fixed-size window: add right, remove right-k"]
  B -- No --> D{"Optimising for?"}
  D -- "Longest valid window" --> E["Grow right; shrink left only when invalid; record max"]
  D -- "Shortest valid window" --> F["Grow right until valid; shrink left while still valid; record min"]
```

Fixed-size is the easiest. The two variable templates differ in one place: for **longest** you shrink only when the window becomes invalid; for **shortest** you shrink aggressively while the window stays valid.

sections.heading: Fixed-size window template
sections.body: When the window size k is fixed (e.g. "maximum sum of any k consecutive elements"), slide by adding the incoming element and subtracting the one that falls off the back. No inner loop needed.

codeExamples.label: Max sum of window size k
codeExamples.code:
def max_sum_k(a, k):
    window = sum(a[:k])
    best = window
    for right in range(k, len(a)):
        window += a[right] - a[right - k]   # add new, drop old
        best = max(best, window)
    return best

sections.heading: Longest-valid-window template
sections.body: Expand `right` every step. When adding `a[right]` breaks the condition, advance `left` (removing elements) until the window is valid again. Record the best length whenever the window is valid. Classic use: 'longest substring without repeating characters', 'longest substring with at most k distinct'.

sections.heading: Shortest-valid-window template
sections.body: Expand `right` until the window first becomes valid (e.g. its sum ≥ target, or it contains all required characters). Then shrink `left` as far as possible *while it stays valid*, recording the minimum length at each step. Classic use: 'minimum size subarray sum', 'minimum window substring'.

codeExamples.label: Minimum size subarray sum >= target
codeExamples.code:
def min_subarray(target, a):
    left = total = 0
    best = float('inf')
    for right, x in enumerate(a):
        total += x
        while total >= target:          # shrink while still valid
            best = min(best, right - left + 1)
            total -= a[left]
            left += 1
    return 0 if best == float('inf') else best

sections.heading: Why it's O(n), and the cost table
sections.body:
Even though there's a nested `while` loop in the variable templates, `left` only ever moves forward and never resets. Across the whole run, `left` advances at most n times total and `right` advances n times — so the work is O(n), not O(n²).

| Variant | Time | Space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed-size (numeric) | O(n) | O(1) |
| Variable + frequency map | O(n) | O(k) for the map |
| Min-window substring | O(n) | O(alphabet) |

The key talking point: 'amortised, each element enters and leaves the window exactly once.'

interviewTalking: Name the trigger out loud: "This asks for a contiguous subarray meeting a condition, so it's a sliding window — not a subsequence DP." Then state which template: "I'll grow the right edge each step and shrink the left edge only when the window becomes invalid, tracking the best length." Close with the O(n) justification: "left and right each move forward at most n times, so it's linear despite the inner loop — O(n) time, O(k) space for the window counter."
commonMistakes: Recomputing the window aggregate from scratch each step (makes it O(n²) — update incrementally instead)
Resetting `left` backward — it must only move forward to keep O(n)
Confusing longest (shrink when invalid) with shortest (shrink while valid) templates
Applying a window to a subsequence problem (windows are contiguous only)
Forgetting to remove the outgoing element from the frequency map when shrinking
complexityNotes: All sliding-window templates are O(n) time because left and right each advance at most n times total. Space is O(1) for numeric windows and O(k) (or O(alphabet)) when maintaining a frequency map of the window's contents.
